lead: An aircraft in service meets lift, weight, thrust, drag, gusts, landings, ground handling and cabin pressure. To size a member, engineers turn the worst service load into a limit load, then multiply by 1.5 to get the ultimate load. The load factor n = L/W says how many times the aircraft’s weight the lift has become: at n = 2.5 the wing lifts 2.5 times the weight. Every wing, fuselage frame and landing gear part is checked against its own critical load case.
prereq: You need: Structural components of aircraft and their functions for load paths and Typical wing and fuselage structures for which member carries bending, shear and pressure.

sections.h3: Sources of load and the load factor

blocks.text: An aircraft carries four main forces: lift L, weight W, thrust T and drag D. In steady level flight L equals W and T equals D. In a pull-up or a gust the lift can become several times the weight, and in a landing the ground reaction on the wheels can.
The load factor n = L / W is dimensionless. L is lift in N and W is weight in N. At n = 1 the lift equals weight; at n = 2.5 the lift is 2.5 times weight. A push-over can give a negative n.

Limit load is the largest load expected in normal service. It is not the failure load. For a wing in symmetric flight, limit lift = n W. For a fuselage, limit load may be cabin pressure plus bending from the tail. For landing gear, it is the vertical impact and spin-up load.

items: Flight loads: lift, weight and inertia, thrust and drag, plus aileron, elevator and rudder loads.
Gust loads: a vertical gust changes the angle of attack and raises lift sharply.
Landing loads: vertical impact, wheel spin-up, braking and side load.
Ground handling: taxi bumps, turning, jacking and towing.

Cabin pressure: the differential pressure p acts on every square metre of skin, giving hoop and longitudinal tension in the shell, and a load of p times the enclosed area on each pressure bulkhead. It is repeated every flight.
Tail loads: the horizontal tail often carries a down-load to balance the wing.

sections.h3: Inertia relief and the net section load

blocks.text: Lift is not the only load on a wing section. In a manoeuvre at load factor n, every mass m on the aircraft pushes down with an inertia load n m g. For a section of the wing, the net load is the aerodynamic load on the outboard part minus the inertia loads of the structure, fuel and engines outboard of that section. The root sees the sum of these net loads. Using lift alone overestimates the bending moment. This is inertia relief.

The same inertia loads act on every seat, galley and fitting in the fuselage, and together with the tail load they bend the fuselage, so each frame station is checked with the masses on either side of it. A heavy engine on a wing relieves root bending in flight because its inertia acts downward against the lift; on landing, when the wing is held up at the gear, the same engine adds to the load. So the critical case for a member depends on mass distribution.

Shear force and bending moment distribution on wings integrates this net load to get shear force and bending moment. For now, remember: the internal load on a section is the net load, not the aerodynamic load alone.

sections.h3: Ultimate load, factor of safety and design criteria

blocks.text: Design uses a factor of safety of 1.5 on the limit load. Ultimate load = 1.5 × limit load. The structure must carry the ultimate load without failure. At limit load it may deflect but must not suffer harmful permanent deformation. The factor covers small variations in load, material and analysis, not gross errors.

blocks.where: P<sub>ult</sub> is ultimate load in N; P<sub>lim</sub> is limit load in N; 1.5 is the aircraft factor of safety, dimensionless.

blocks.text: A critical load case is the combination of loads that gives the highest stress in a particular member. A wing spar may be critical in a gust at high speed; a fuselage frame may be critical under pressure plus bending; landing gear is critical at touchdown. Each member is sized for its own critical case.

items: Safe-life: the part is given a fixed life and retired before cracks are expected. Used for landing gear and some helicopter parts.
Fail-safe: the structure has multiple load paths or crack stoppers, so one failed member does not cause collapse.
Damage tolerance: the structure is designed so cracks grow slowly and are found by inspection before they become dangerous. Used for modern transport wings and fuselages.

examples.question: An aircraft of mass 60 000 kg is designed for a manoeuvre load factor of 2.5. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the limit lift and the ultimate load for the wing. State the factor of safety used.
steps: Limit lift L<sub>lim</sub> = n W = 2.5 × 588.6 = 1 471.5 kN = 1.4715 MN ≈ 1.47 MN.
The aircraft factor of safety is 1.5.
examples.answer: Limit lift = 1.47 MN; ultimate load = 2.21 MN.
examples.check:
m = 60000
g = 9.81
n = 2.5
W = m * g
limit = n * W / 1e6
ult = 1.5 * limit
print(round(limit, 2))
print(round(ult, 2))

examples.question: A wing-mounted engine of mass 2000 kg sits 4.0 m outboard of the wing root. In a pull-up at n = 2.5, the lift outboard of the root gives a root bending moment of 1800 kN·m. Find the engine’s inertia load, the bending moment it removes at the root, and the net root bending moment. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Inertia load of the engine: F = n m g = 2.5 × 2000 × 9.81 = 49 050 N = 49.05 kN, acting downward.
Relief moment at the root: F × arm = 49.05 kN × 4.0 m = 196.2 kN·m, opposite in sense to the lift moment.
examples.answer: The engine pushes down with 49.05 kN and removes 196.2 kN·m, so the root sees about 1604 kN·m, 11 % less than lift alone would give.

traps: Applying the 1.5 factor of safety twice, for example to an ultimate load that is already factored.
Using the full aerodynamic lift as the root bending load and forgetting inertia relief.
Writing kN and MN in the same line without converting: 588.6 kN = 0.5886 MN.
Calling the limit load the failure load; the structure must not fail at ultimate, which is 1.5 times limit.
Confusing load factor n with factor of safety 1.5; n is a service load ratio, 1.5 is a design multiplier.

quiz.q: Define limit load and ultimate load.
quiz.a: Limit load is the largest load expected in service. Ultimate load is 1.5 times the limit load and the structure must not fail at it.

quiz.q: Write the formula for load factor and state its units.
quiz.a: n = L/W; n is dimensionless, L and W are in N.

quiz.q: Why is the root bending moment of a wing not simply lift times the semi-span?
quiz.a: Inertia of the wing, fuel and engines acts downward and relieves the net load; the internal moment comes from the integral of net load, not lift alone.

quiz.q: An aircraft of mass 20 000 kg has n = 3. Find limit lift and ultimate load. Use g = 9.81 m/s².
A wing carries fuel. Explain how the fuel changes the critical load case for the wing root.
quiz.a: In flight fuel inertia relieves root bending, so a light-fuel case can be more critical for upward bending. On landing the fuel mass adds downward load, so a full-fuel landing can be critical for the root and landing gear.

quiz.q: Give one difference between safe-life and fail-safe design.
quiz.a: Safe-life retires a part after a fixed life with no crack assumed; fail-safe provides alternate load paths so one failure does not collapse the structure.

quiz.q: A member has an ultimate load of 2.21 MN. What is its limit load?
Why does a vertical gust produce a sharp increase in wing load, and which flight speed is likely critical?
quiz.a: A gust changes the local angle of attack, so lift rises quickly. The extra load factor grows with speed times gust velocity. The design gust is smaller at the dive speed than at the cruise speed, so the cruise-speed gust usually gives the largest load factor, as the V-n diagram shows.

quiz.q: A fuel load of 3000 kg acts 3.0 m outboard of a wing root. Find the root bending relief it gives at n = 2.5 (g = 9.81 m/s²).

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, loads come from a loads survey that combines flight test, wind tunnel and CFD. Certification checks a spectrum of loads over the life, not one number, and fatigue and damage tolerance are part of the case. Modern work adds digital twins and sensor-based load monitoring. Search for 'flight loads survey', 'gust load alleviation' and 'damage tolerance inspection'.
